abstract: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are a widespread class of translated regions (translons) occurring in 5' leaders of messenger RNAs. They serve critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation and some are known to encode small proteins and peptideins. Yet it is not known which of these modes of function is more critical for human cells. We conducted a CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis screening targeting 969 translated human uORFs across three cell lines of distinct origin. Disruption of 155 uORFs impaired cell proliferation, although these effects were highly cell-type specific, with only six shared across all cell lines. Neither evolutionary conservation, comparative protein-coding potential, nor population mutational constraint distinguished uORF hits. Instead, high-throughput analysis of CRISPR-induced mutations combined with reporter assays demonstrated that proliferation phenotypes arise from altered cis-regulation of coding sequence (CDS) translation. In particular, uORFs located within short 5' leaders were disproportionately sensitive to indels, which frequently changed the uORF-CDS configuration, resulting in altered gene expression. We further identified naturally occurring human variants that are predicted to perturb these uORFs-CDS configurations, potentially contributing to disease phenotypes. Together, these findings identify uORF translation as a pervasive layer of gene-expression control. This study demonstrates that for most uORFs, it is their native translation rather than the activity of their products that is critical for the proliferation of human cells. It also provides a systematic resource for investigating uORF functions.

summary: CRISPR-Cas9 screen of 969 human uORFs across three cell lines finds proliferation effects arise from altered CDS translation cis-regulation, not uORF products.
title: Translons upstream of protein-coding regions rather than their products are crucial for proliferation of human cells of distinct origin.
